rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the full elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing retained compounds. A moderate temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.
Change only gradient duration to measure how the two critical early pairs respond to slope. This diagnostic run will guide subsequent window trimming and temperature tuning.

The shallower gradient improved the critical cluster but incurred a time penalty. Test higher temperature at the original slope to shift selectivity and shorten retention without sacrificing that time advantage.

At 60 C only one pair remains below target, with nearly two minutes of retention-time headroom. A shallower gradient should test whether that pair can reach baseline resolution while keeping the last peak close to 10 minutes.

The remaining critical pair worsened with a shallower gradient, so test a steeper slope instead. This should improve that pair and shorten the run, while checking that its neighboring pair retains sufficient resolution.

Slope changes alone have not resolved the remaining pair. Raise the starting organic fraction to test selectivity in the early cluster, using a moderate gradient duration to preserve spacing and monitoring the first peak for inadequate retention.
Injection 6 reached the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark and shorten the gradient by one step. This tests whether full resolution can be maintained with a faster last-peak elution.

Shorten the gradient one more step to locate the full-resolution speed limit at this solvent window. Injection 7 remains the faster validated maximum-score method if either critical pair falls below 1.5.

Narrow the gradient window to recover the small resolution deficits at eight minutes. The resulting slope lies between injections 7 and 8, and the endpoint remains comfortably above the last peak’s estimated elution composition.

Test whether a further increase in starting organic fraction improves the critical cluster enough to permit faster elution. Monitor early-peak retention and resolution closely; injection 9 remains the fastest validated fully resolved method.

Test temperature selectivity around the fastest fully resolved method, changing only temperature. This will show whether a modest decrease creates resolution headroom for further gradient compression.

Return to 60 C and test a slope just steeper than injection 9, targeting the boundary of full resolution. The endpoint remains slightly above the estimated last-peak elution composition, so the shorter programmed gradient should still capture all peaks during the ramp.

Injection 12 still has a pair below 1.5 despite its rounded CRF of 1.000, so injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method. Test a shallower gradient at phi0 0.20 to determine whether its limiting pair can recover while preserving the improved neighboring separation.

With maximum CRF already secured, test the opposite temperature extreme for a different selectivity regime that might support a faster fully resolved method. The strong endpoint and eight-minute ramp limit the risk of an excessively retained last peak.

The low-temperature regime substantially worsened selectivity, so return to 60 C. Test a shallower gradient to increase the minimum-resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes and retaining maximum CRF.

Back off one endpoint step from injection 12 to recover its marginally deficient pair while retaining a six-minute programmed gradient. The last peak may approach the start of the hold, so verify both complete elution and full resolution.

At phi0 0.20, increasing tG from 8 to 12 minutes improved the limiting pair to 1.47. One further duration step should test whether this alternative window reaches full resolution below 10 minutes; injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test the remaining starting-composition grid point between 0.05 and 0.15 at a fast gradient. This checks whether the early cluster has a better selectivity balance there, while retaining injection 9 as the fastest validated maximum-score method.

The tested starting compositions favor phi0 0.15, and injection 9 remains the fastest fully resolved method. Test a shallower slope for a larger resolution margin while aiming to keep the last peak below the 10-minute penalty threshold.

Refine around injection 9 by lowering the endpoint one grid step, aiming for a little more resolution margin with only a modest increase in retention time. This offers a faster alternative to the more conservative fully resolved methods.

Refine the full-resolution boundary at phi0 0.20 using a slope between injections 13 and 17. This tests whether that alternative window can retain maximum CRF with a shorter last-peak time than injection 17.

Shorten injection 19’s gradient by four minutes to seek a faster maximum-score method with more resolution margin than injection 9. The resulting slope lies within the experimentally confirmed full-resolution range.

Trim injection 22’s window while preserving its gradient slope and early-pair separation. The last peak should elute near the start of the final hold; verify that the shorter programmed gradient retains full resolution without appreciably delaying it.

Test a compromise between injection 9’s speed and injection 15’s resolution margin, aiming to retain maximum CRF with less sensitivity to the critical pair. Injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Preserve injection 9’s slope and early critical-pair separation while testing a four-minute ramp followed by a hold. Verify whether the late peaks still elute within 10 minutes; injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method with maximum CRF.
